title: The Guests That Stayed
topic: endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts
paragraphs: Nearly every cell of a plant, animal, or fungus carries mitochondria, small compartments that burn sugar with oxygen to power the cell, and plant and algal cells also carry chloroplasts, which capture sunlight.
Both, by the account now in every textbook, began as free-living bacteria that were swallowed by another cell more than a billion years ago and never left.
That account, the endosymbiotic theory, is so settled today that it is easy to forget how long it spent as a joke.
How it was proposed, mocked, forgotten, revived, and finally proved is a lesson in how evidence, rather than argument, moves a science.
The first hints came from the microscope.

In 1883 the German botanist Andreas Schimper observed that chloroplasts are never built from scratch but arise only when an existing chloroplast splits in two, and he remarked in passing that green plants might have begun as a partnership between a colorless organism and a chlorophyll-bearing one.
The Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski took the remark seriously.
He had spent years studying lichens, in which a fungus and an alga live as one body, and the lichen gave him a model for how two organisms might merge into one.
In 1905 he proposed that chloroplasts had begun as cyanobacteria taken in by a host cell, and in 1910 he coined the word symbiogenesis for the making of new life forms by merger.
The idea for mitochondria arrived a generation later, and in worse company.
In the 1920s the American anatomist Ivan Wallin argued that mitochondria were bacteria and reported that he had grown them in culture outside the cell.
No one else could repeat the result, and the failure tainted the larger claim with the smaller.
Few biologists were willing to entertain the proposal after that.

In 1925 the American cell biologist Edmund Beecher Wilson wrote that such speculations seemed too fantastic for polite biological society, though he allowed that they might someday deserve serious thought.
For nearly four decades they did not get it.
What changed the mood was not an argument but a finding.
In 1962 Hans Ris and Walter Plaut showed with the electron microscope that the chloroplast of the green alga Chlamydomonas contains DNA of its own.
The following year Margit Nass and Sylvan Nass reported fibers with the properties of DNA inside the mitochondria of chick embryos.
An organelle with its own genes looked less like a part than a resident, and the old speculation had something to stand on.
The biologist who built on that footing was Lynn Margulis.
In 1967, not yet thirty and publishing under her married name, Lynn Sagan, she placed a long paper, On the Origin of Mitosing Cells, in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.
It is said to have been turned down by about fifteen journals first.

It argued that mitochondria descended from oxygen-breathing bacteria, that chloroplasts descended from cyanobacteria, and, more boldly, that the whiplike tails many eukaryotic cells swim with had descended from spirochetes, a group of corkscrew-shaped bacteria.
She expanded the case in a 1970 book, Origin of Eukaryotic Cells, and the package was named serial endosymbiosis, because the mergers were supposed to have happened one after another.
The reception was cool, and the coolness was not entirely unfair.
A theory of ancient mergers predicts that the organelles should resemble particular bacteria in their molecules, and in 1967 there was no good way to check.
The tools arrived over the next two decades, largely through Carl Woese, who showed that ribosomal RNA, a molecule every cell carries, could be used to trace kinship among microbes.

When the organelles' own ribosomal RNA was read, mitochondria fell among the alpha-proteobacteria, a group that includes the typhus bacterium Rickettsia, and chloroplasts fell squarely among the cyanobacteria.
By the mid-1980s the organelle half of Margulis's theory was textbook material; she was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1983 and received the National Medal of Science in 1999.
The spirochete half never found comparable support, and I think the two halves deserve different grades: filing them under one name does her real achievement no favor.
The classic case rests on four lines of evidence.
First, both carry DNA of their own, typically a circular molecule like a bacterial chromosome, not the linear kind in the nucleus.
Second, both are enclosed by two membranes rather than one.
Third, both make some of their own proteins on ribosomes that resemble bacterial ribosomes more than those in the surrounding cytoplasm.
Fourth, both reproduce by pinching in two, the way bacteria divide, and a cell that loses them cannot build new ones.
The genomes are small, because most of the original bacterial genes have moved to the nucleus or been lost.
Human mitochondrial DNA is 16,569 base pairs long and holds 37 genes, of which 13 encode proteins; the rest encode the RNAs needed to make those 13.

A typical land plant chloroplast genome is larger, roughly 120,000 to 160,000 base pairs and a hundred or so genes, but it too is a remnant beside the several thousand genes of a free-living cyanobacterium.
The missing proteins are made in the cytoplasm and imported: a human mitochondrion takes in more than a thousand different proteins and makes only 13 itself.
To my mind the ribosome evidence is the most persuasive, because it can be tested with a bottle of antibiotics.

Chloramphenicol, which halts protein synthesis in bacteria by binding their ribosomes, also halts protein synthesis inside mitochondria and chloroplasts while leaving the cell's cytoplasmic ribosomes untouched.
Cycloheximide does the reverse: it stops the cytoplasmic ribosomes and spares both the organelles and the bacteria.
A borrowed machine keeps the habits of its maker.
The membranes deserve more caution than they usually get.
The tidy textbook drawing makes the inner membrane the bacterium's own and the outer one the pouch of host membrane that closed around it when it was swallowed.

But a mitochondrion's outer membrane is studded with porins, barrel-shaped channels of the kind found in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, and the bacteria mitochondria descend from are gram-negative, with two membranes of their own.
On that evidence the outer membrane may be bacterial as well, and the host's pouch, if there ever was one, may have been lost rather than kept.
Division tells a similar story of inheritance with revision.
Chloroplasts split using FtsZ, the same protein that assembles into a ring at the middle of a dividing bacterium and draws it in two.

The mitochondria of animals and fungi have lost FtsZ and are pinched instead by a protein borrowed from the host cell's membrane-cutting toolkit, though a few algae still divide their mitochondria with the bacterial ring.
The guest, in other words, has been remodeled by the house, and the extent of remodeling records how long the arrangement has lasted.
The experiment has also been run again, which is the strongest kind of evidence a historical theory can get.

Several groups of algae got their chloroplasts by swallowing not a cyanobacterium but a eukaryotic alga that already had one, and their chloroplasts sit inside three or four membranes rather than two, the extra layers being the remains of the engulfed cell.

More striking is a freshwater amoeba called Paulinella, which took in a cyanobacterium on its own, independently of the plant lineage and much more recently, on the order of a hundred million years ago.
Its partner still has a genome several times larger than any chloroplast's, as if the merger had been caught midway.
Why did a correct idea wait sixty years for a hearing?
It is tempting to cast Mereschkowski as a prophet wronged by a timid profession, and I do not think that is quite right.
His proposal rested on resemblance, and resemblance is a weak witness: plenty of things divide by splitting without being bacteria.
Wallin's irreproducible cultures made matters worse, and until 1962 there was no fact in hand that resemblance alone could not explain.

The lesson is less flattering and more useful: a right answer can sit unproven for a lifetime, and the credit is fairly shared with whoever builds the instrument that finally asks the question properly.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Schimper observed in 1883 that chloroplasts
choices: contain DNA of their own, like a bacterial chromosome
arise only when an existing chloroplast splits
resemble the alga that lives inside a lichen
can be grown in culture apart from the cell
are enclosed by two membranes rather than one

proof.quote: arise only when an existing chloroplast splits in two

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says Schimper observed that chloroplasts are never assembled from scratch but arise only when an existing chloroplast splits in two. That continuity was the first hint.
distractorNotes: Wrong era: DNA inside chloroplasts was not shown until Ris and Plaut in 1962, in paragraph 4.
Mash-up: lichens belong to Mereschkowski in paragraph 2, and no one says chloroplasts resemble the lichen's alga.
Wrong person and organelle: culturing outside the cell was Wallin's claim about mitochondria in paragraph 3.
Wrong paragraph: the double membrane is listed as evidence in paragraph 7, not as Schimper's observation.

questions.stem: The author mentions lichens in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: show that Schimper and Mereschkowski studied the same organisms
introduce the first organism known to contain a chloroplast
explain why cyanobacteria could survive inside a host cell
identify where Mereschkowski found a model for a merger
argue that fungi, like plants, descended from a bacterial partner

proof.quote: the lichen gave him a model for how two organisms might merge into one

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says Mereschkowski had spent years studying lichens, in which a fungus and an alga live as a single body, and that the lichen gave him a model for how two organisms might merge. The lichen is there to explain where his idea came from.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: Schimper is tied to chloroplasts in paragraph 2, not to lichens.
Outside the passage: nothing says lichens were the first organisms known to hold chloroplasts.
Wrong function: the lichen is a model for partnership, not an explanation of how a cyanobacterium survives inside a host.
Too strong: the passage never claims that fungi descended from a bacterial partnership.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the claim by Ivan Wallin that no one else could repeat was that he had
choices: grown mitochondria in culture outside the cell
found DNA fibers inside the mitochondria of chick embryos
traced mitochondria to the alpha-proteobacteria
shown that mitochondria reproduce by pinching in two
persuaded Wilson that mitochondria were bacteria

proof.quote: reported that he had grown them in culture outside the cell
No one else could repeat the result

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Wallin reported that he had grown mitochondria in culture outside the cell, and that no one else could repeat the result.
distractorNotes: Wrong people and decade: the DNA fibers were reported by Margit and Sylvan Nass in 1963, in paragraph 4.
Wrong era: ribosomal RNA sequencing placed mitochondria there decades later, in paragraph 6.
Wrong source: division by pinching is one of the four lines of evidence in paragraph 7, not Wallin's experiment.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says Wilson found such speculations too fantastic for polite biological society.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Wilson's remark in 1925 was
choices: a direct reply to the paper Margulis would later publish
the main reason the idea stayed dormant for decades
a defense of Wallin's attempts to culture mitochondria
an endorsement of Mereschkowski's proposal about chloroplasts
a dismissal that left room for a later change of mind

proof.quote: though he allowed that they might someday deserve serious thought

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Wilson called such speculations too fantastic for polite biological society, though he allowed that they might someday deserve serious thought. He dismissed the idea for the present without closing the door on it.
distractorNotes: Impossible timing: Margulis's paper came in 1967, more than forty years after the remark.
Too strong: paragraph 3 blames Wallin's unrepeatable result, and paragraph 13 blames the lack of any testable fact, not Wilson's remark.
Reversed: Wilson's remark belittled such speculations rather than defending them.
Reversed: calling an idea too fantastic for polite society is not an endorsement.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Margit Nass and Sylvan Nass reported
choices: that the chloroplast of Chlamydomonas contains DNA of its own
that mitochondria could be cultured apart from the cell
fibers with the properties of DNA inside mitochondria
that organelle ribosomes are blocked by chloramphenicol
that mitochondrial DNA forms a single circular molecule

proof.quote: reported fibers with the properties of DNA inside the mitochondria of chick embryos

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says that in 1963 Margit Nass and Sylvan Nass reported fibers with the properties of DNA inside the mitochondria of chick embryos.
distractorNotes: Wrong team: the Chlamydomonas chloroplast finding belongs to Ris and Plaut in 1962.
Wrong person: that was Wallin's unrepeatable claim in paragraph 3.
Wrong paragraph: the chloramphenicol test appears in paragraph 9 and is not credited to the Nasses.
Wrong paragraph: the circular shape is described in paragraph 7, not as the Nass finding.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Margulis's 1967 paper
choices: appeared under the name Lynn Sagan
was published in a book titled Origin of Eukaryotic Cells
was accepted by the first journal that considered it
argued that chloroplasts descended from spirochetes
was written after she joined the National Academy

proof.quote: publishing under her married name, Lynn Sagan

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says she published the 1967 paper under her married name, Lynn Sagan, in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.
distractorNotes: Mash-up: the book came in 1970; the 1967 paper appeared in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.
Reversed: paragraph 5 says it was turned down by about fifteen journals first.
Mash-up: spirochetes were proposed as the source of swimming tails and hairs, not of chloroplasts.
Reversed chronology: paragraph 6 says she was elected in 1983, long after the paper.

questions.stem: All of the following are stated in the passage about Margulis's theory EXCEPT:
choices: It held that mitochondria descended from oxygen-breathing bacteria.
It held that chloroplasts descended from cyanobacteria.
Its mergers were supposed to have happened one after another.
Its organelle half was textbook material by the mid-1980s.
Its spirochete half was confirmed by ribosomal RNA sequencing.

proof.quote: mitochondria descended from oxygen-breathing bacteria
chloroplasts descended from cyanobacteria
the mergers were supposed to have happened one after another
By the mid-1980s the organelle half of Margulis's theory was textbook material
The spirochete half never found comparable support

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the spirochete half never found comparable support. The other four statements come straight from paragraphs 5 and 6.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 5 as the first of the paper's three claims.
Stated in paragraph 5 as the second of the paper's claims.
Stated in paragraph 5 as the reason for the name serial endosymbiosis.
Stated in paragraph 6, in the same sentence as her election to the National Academy.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the organelle half of Margulis's theory won acceptance mainly because
choices: Margulis had been elected to the National Academy of Sciences
tools arriving after 1967 let its prediction be tested
Rickettsia was shown to be the agent of typhus
Carl Woese publicly endorsed the serial endosymbiosis theory
the spirochete half of the theory had already been confirmed

proof.quote: in 1967 there was no good way to check
The tools arrived over the next two decades
By the mid-1980s the organelle half of Margulis's theory was textbook material

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the theory made a prediction that could not be checked in 1967, that the tools arrived over the next two decades, and that once the organelles' ribosomal RNA was read the organelle half became textbook material. Acceptance followed the test.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the election in 1983 came as the theory was being accepted, not as its cause.
Irrelevant detail: Rickettsia is mentioned only as a relative of mitochondria, not as a reason for acceptance.
Outside the passage: Woese is credited with the ribosomal RNA method, not with endorsing the theory.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 says the spirochete half never found comparable support.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the spirochete half of Margulis's theory is best described as
choices: admiring
indignant
unconvinced
disappointed
ambivalent

proof.quote: The spirochete half never found comparable support, and I think the two halves deserve different grades

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the spirochete half never found comparable support and that the two halves deserve different grades. The author is not persuaded by that half, and says so plainly.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author's admiration goes to the organelle half, which the spirochete half is set against.
Wrong register: the author is calm and measured, not angry.
Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 6 expresses regret or let-down, only a verdict on the evidence.
Too weak: the author gives a clear verdict rather than wavering between views.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 7, all of the following are among the classic lines of evidence for the theory EXCEPT:
choices: DNA of their own, typically circular
ribosomes that resemble bacterial ribosomes
reproduction by pinching in two
enclosure by two membranes rather than one
a genome larger than a bacterium's

proof.quote: both carry DNA of their own, typically a circular molecule
ribosomes that resemble bacterial ribosomes
both reproduce by pinching in two
both are enclosed by two membranes rather than one
The genomes are small

questions.why: Paragraph 7 lists four lines: their own DNA, two membranes, bacteria-like ribosomes, and division by pinching in two. Paragraph 8 says the genomes are small, remnants beside a free-living bacterium's, so a large genome is the opposite of what the passage says.
distractorNotes: Listed first in paragraph 7.
Listed third in paragraph 7.
Listed fourth in paragraph 7.
Listed second in paragraph 7.

questions.stem: According to the passage, human mitochondrial DNA
choices: is roughly 120,000 to 160,000 base pairs long
encodes more than a thousand different proteins
carries a hundred or so genes
holds 37 genes, of which 13 encode proteins
is several times larger than a chloroplast genome

proof.quote: holds 37 genes, of which 13 encode proteins

questions.why: Paragraph 8 gives the figures: human mitochondrial DNA is 16,569 base pairs long and holds 37 genes, of which 13 encode proteins.
distractorNotes: Wrong organelle: that range is the land plant chloroplast genome in paragraph 8.
Reversed: paragraph 8 says the mitochondrion imports more than a thousand proteins and makes only 13 itself.
Wrong organelle: a hundred or so genes is the chloroplast figure in paragraph 8.
Reversed: the chloroplast genome is the larger one; the several-times-larger genome belongs to Paulinella's partner in paragraph 12.

questions.stem: A newly discovered antibiotic halts protein synthesis in bacteria by binding to their ribosomes. If the antibiotic were added to living plant cells, which outcome does the rule in paragraph 9 predict?
choices: Synthesis would halt everywhere in the cell, because all of its ribosomes are the same kind
Synthesis would halt inside the organelles but continue in the cytoplasm
Synthesis would halt in the cytoplasm but continue inside the organelles
The organelles would stop dividing, because division depends on bacterial ribosomes
Nothing would change, because antibiotics act only on free-living bacteria

proof.quote: also halts protein synthesis inside mitochondria and chloroplasts while leaving the cell's cytoplasmic ribosomes untouched
A borrowed machine keeps the habits of its maker.

questions.why: Paragraph 9's rule is that a drug which binds bacterial ribosomes, like chloramphenicol, also halts protein synthesis inside mitochondria and chloroplasts while leaving the cytoplasmic ribosomes untouched. A new antibiotic that works the same way should sort the cell the same way.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 9 says the cytoplasmic ribosomes are left untouched because they are a different kind.
Reversed: that is the cycloheximide pattern, the opposite of a bacterial ribosome blocker.
Outside the passage: paragraph 9 is about protein synthesis, and division is handled by FtsZ and its substitutes in paragraph 11.
Contradicted: the whole point of paragraph 9 is that the organelles respond like bacteria.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 3, the word 'entertain' most nearly means
choices: give serious consideration to
amuse with a performance
host as a guest in one's home
defend in public against critics
keep alive for a long time

proof.quote: Few biologists were willing to entertain the proposal after that.

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says few biologists were willing to entertain the proposal after Wallin's result failed. To entertain a proposal is to consider it seriously; the sentence is about ideas, not amusement.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning, but a proposal is not a show, and the sentence is about taking an idea seriously.
Hosting a guest is another common meaning that makes no sense with a proposal as the object.
Too strong: the sentence is about mere willingness to consider the idea, not public defense of it.
Wrong sense: the passage says the idea went unconsidered, not that it was kept alive.

questions.stem: According to the passage, chloroplasts divide using
choices: a protein borrowed from the host cell's membrane-cutting toolkit
porins of the kind found in gram-negative bacteria
the same protein that forms a ring in a dividing bacterium
a mechanism that has been lost in every alga
ribosomes that resemble those of bacteria

proof.quote: Chloroplasts split using FtsZ, the same protein that assembles into a ring at the middle of a dividing bacterium

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says chloroplasts split using FtsZ, the same protein that assembles into a ring at the middle of a dividing bacterium and draws it in two.
distractorNotes: Wrong organelle: the host's membrane-cutting protein pinches the mitochondria of animals and fungi.
Wrong paragraph: porins sit in the mitochondrial outer membrane in paragraph 10 and have nothing to do with division.
Reversed: paragraph 11 says a few algae still use the bacterial ring even for their mitochondria.
Wrong line: ribosomes are evidence about protein synthesis, not the machinery of division.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an alga whose chloroplast is wrapped in four membranes most likely
choices: took in a cyanobacterium more recently than plants did
is a close relative of the amoeba Paulinella
has a chloroplast genome several times larger than usual
acquired its chloroplast by engulfing another eukaryote
lost the two membranes that its ancestors originally had

proof.quote: their chloroplasts sit inside three or four membranes rather than two, the extra layers being the remains of the engulfed cell

questions.why: Paragraph 12 says some algae got their chloroplasts by swallowing a whole eukaryotic alga that already had one, and that such chloroplasts sit inside three or four membranes, the extra layers being the remains of the engulfed cell. Four membranes point to that second route.
distractorNotes: Wrong case: the recent, independent uptake of a cyanobacterium is Paulinella's story, and it involves no extra membranes.
Outside the passage: nothing links the four-membrane algae to Paulinella.
Wrong case: the oversized genome belongs to Paulinella's partner, not to secondhand chloroplasts.
Reversed: the four-membrane chloroplast has gained layers, not lost them.

questions.stem: The author mentions Paulinella in paragraph 12 primarily to
choices: show that amoebas, like plants, can carry out photosynthesis
argue that chloroplasts arose more recently than mitochondria
explain why some chloroplasts sit inside three or four membranes
show that a merger can be reversed once it has begun
offer an independent and more recent instance of the same event

proof.quote: The experiment has also been run again, which is the strongest kind of evidence a historical theory can get.
which took in a cyanobacterium on its own, independently of the plant lineage and much more recently

questions.why: Paragraph 12 opens by saying the experiment has been run again, the strongest evidence a historical theory can get, and Paulinella is its most striking example: a cyanobacterium taken in independently of plants and much more recently.
distractorNotes: Half right at best: Paulinella's partner is a cyanobacterium, but the paragraph is about repetition of the merger, not about which organisms photosynthesize.
Outside the passage: no comparison of the ages of chloroplasts and mitochondria is made.
Wrong sentence: the extra membranes are explained by the swallowing of a eukaryotic alga, before Paulinella appears.
Contradicted: the merger is described as caught midway, not reversed.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Lynn Margulis was the first scientist to propose that mitochondria and chloroplasts had descended from free-living bacteria
An idea long dismissed, that organelles began as swallowed bacteria, was vindicated once evidence could test it
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are the only parts of the cell that contain DNA of their own
Biologists of the early twentieth century were too timid to accept a correct idea about the cell
Antibiotics provide the only reliable test of whether an organelle was once a free-living bacterium

proof.quote: began as free-living bacteria that were swallowed by another cell more than a billion years ago and never left
a lesson in how evidence, rather than argument, moves a science
a right answer can sit unproven for a lifetime

questions.why: Paragraph 1 states the theory and frames the passage as a lesson in how evidence, rather than argument, moves a science; paragraph 13 closes on the same note. The body traces the dismissal, the revival, and the molecular proof.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 2 credits Mereschkowski in 1905, and paragraph 3 credits Wallin for mitochondria, both before Margulis.
Too narrow and never claimed: the nucleus also holds DNA, and the organelles' DNA is one of several lines of evidence.
Reversed: paragraph 13 says the author does not think the profession's hesitation was simply timidity.
Too strong: paragraph 9 calls the antibiotic test the most persuasive, not the only reliable one.
